stages.title: Hear up and down
stages.about: Before singing, train your ear to hear whether a note goes up or down. Every answer is shown as a picture.

chapters.title: Watch it move
chapters.hint: Listen and watch. Higher on the screen means higher in pitch.

lessons.title: Big jumps, with pictures
lessons.theory: Pitch is how high or low a note sounds. Here each note appears as a dot when it plays, so you can see the jump while you hear it. These two notes are a whole octave apart, the biggest jump in this course.

lessons.title: Sa and Pa, with pictures
lessons.theory: Sa to Pa is a smaller jump, but still a clear one. Watch which way the line points: up means the second note is higher, down means lower.

chapters.title: Up or down?
chapters.hint: Listen first, then answer. The picture appears after you choose.

lessons.title: Octave jumps
lessons.theory: Now the picture waits until you answer. Many people find it easier to hum the two notes back quietly before choosing.

lessons.title: Sa to Pa jumps
lessons.theory: If you are unsure, imagine the notes as steps on a staircase: is the second step above or below the first?

lessons.title: Medium jumps
lessons.theory: These jumps are smaller, like Sa to Ma or Sa to Ga. Your ear gets sharper with every round, even the ones you miss.

lessons.title: Small steps
lessons.theory: Neighbouring swarams, like Sa and Ri, are the hardest to tell apart. Take your time and hear each pair as often as you like.

lessons.title: All sizes mixed
lessons.theory: Big and small jumps mixed together. This is what real melodies do: every song is a chain of ups and downs.

chapters.title: Up, down or the same?
chapters.hint: Sometimes the note stays where it is.

lessons.title: Up, down or same
lessons.theory: A repeated note is as important as a moving one; Janta Varasas later are built on it. Listen for whether the second note moves at all.

lessons.title: Small steps or same
lessons.theory: The finest listening test here: a small step or no step at all. Passing this means your ear is ready to guide your voice.

chapters.title: Sing it up, sing it down
chapters.hint: Now sing. Watch your own line on the graph climb or fall like the reference.

lessons.title: Climb to Pa
lessons.theory: Your voice draws a line on the graph as you sing. When you go from Sa to Pa, your line should climb, just like the dots did.

lessons.title: Fall to Sa
lessons.theory: Now the other way. Going down, many voices stop short of the target; let your line fall all the way to the Sa rung.

lessons.title: Climb an octave
lessons.theory: Upper Sa is the same note, higher. Your line should jump a long way up and then sit flat.

lessons.title: Fall an octave
lessons.theory: From upper Sa back home. Seeing your line land on Sa is the clearest proof that your ear and voice agree.

stages.title: Find your voice
stages.about: One note at a time. No rhythm to keep up with and nothing to memorise.

chapters.title: One note at a time
chapters.hint: Breathe in, then hold each note for four slow beats.

lessons.theory: Sa is Shadjam, which means 'born of six': the other six swarams grow out of it. Old texts liken it to the call of a peacock. Every song you will ever sing returns home to Sa.
Ri is Rishabham, the swaram texts liken to the call of a bull. It is the first step away from home, so it should feel like a small, sure step, not a stretch.
Ga is Gandharam, likened to the bleat of a goat. With Sa and Ri it forms the first small climb you will sing, and it gives a scale its bright or dark colour.
Ma is Madhyamam, 'the middle one': it sits at the centre of the seven swarams. Old texts liken it to the cry of the krauncha bird, the heron.
Pa is Panchamam, the fifth, likened to the song of the koel. Sa and Pa never change in any ragam, which is why the tambura plays only Sa and Pa.

stages.title: Small steps
stages.about: Move between neighbouring notes. Every phrase starts and ends somewhere you have already been.

chapters.title: Two notes
chapters.hint: Step to the next note, then back.

lessons.theory: Moving between two neighbouring swarams is called a step. A clean step lands straight on the new note, like stepping onto a stair, instead of sliding up a ramp.
Coming down is often harder than going up: the voice tends to fall flat. Think of placing Sa gently, as if setting down a full glass.
Sa Ri Sa is a tiny round trip. Every phrase in Carnatic music is built from journeys like this one, away from home and back again.
Here home moves to Ri. Practising the same shape from different swarams trains your ear to hear the distance, not just the names.
Ga to Ma is a smaller step than Ri to Ga, a half step instead of a whole one. Listen for how much closer together they feel.
Ma Pa Ma crosses the middle of the scale. Pa is fixed in every ragam, so it is a safe place to land.

chapters.title: Three notes
chapters.hint: Climb three notes and come back down.

lessons.theory: Three rising swarams make the smallest arohanam, the ascent. Ragam Mohanam is built on just five swarams and starts the same way: Sa Ri Ga.
The descent is called avarohanam. Every ragam is defined by its own arohanam and avarohanam, a little like a signature.
The same shape, one swaram higher. Your voice may feel slightly different here; that is your range changing, and it is completely normal.
Let each swaram finish before the next begins. Teachers call this clarity swara shuddhi, clean notes.
Ga Ma Pa spans the middle of the octave. This is often the most comfortable part of the voice, so enjoy it.
Coming down from Pa, keep the energy in the voice even though the notes get lower. Flat endings are the most common slip at this stage.

stages.title: The scale, piece by piece
stages.about: Build the full scale from the lower half and the upper half before joining them.

chapters.title: The lower half
chapters.hint: Keep every note even as the phrase grows.

lessons.theory: Sa Ri Ga Ma is the purvanga, the first half of the scale. Many ragams can be recognised from this half alone.
Walking back down the purvanga. If Sa sounds lower than when you started, pause, play Sa again and match it.
Adding Pa completes five swarams. Five-note ragams such as Mohanam and Hamsadhwani are among the most loved in Carnatic music.
Five notes down to Sa. You have now sung more than half of every scale you will ever learn.

chapters.title: The upper half
chapters.hint: The same steps, higher up. Reach the upper Sa without pushing.

lessons.theory: Pa to Da begins the uttaranga, the upper half of the scale. It mirrors the lower half, Sa to Ri, one Pa higher.
Da is Dhaivatam, likened to the neigh of a horse, and Ni is Nishadam, likened to the trumpet of an elephant.
Ni to upper Sa is another half step. Ni always wants to resolve upward into Sa; let it.
Upper Sa vibrates exactly twice as fast as lower Sa. That is why they sound like the same note, one sthayi, or octave, apart.
Coming down from upper Sa, keep your voice light at the top. Pushing makes the voice tight and the pitch sharp.

chapters.title: The whole scale
chapters.hint: Join the two halves you already know.

lessons.swaras: S R G M P D N S'
lessons.theory: These eight notes, with Ma and Ni as you have sung them, form Dheerasankarabharanam, the 29th of the 72 melakarta ragams. Its notes match the Western major scale.

lessons.swaras: S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: The complete avarohanam. Traditionally the first lessons are taught in Mayamalavagowla; we use Sankarabharanam here because its notes are easier for a new ear.

chapters.title: Small leaps
chapters.hint: Land on the note without sliding up to it.

lessons.theory: A leap skips over swarams. Hear Ga in your head before you sing it, then land on it directly without sliding.
Sa to Pa is the most natural leap in music: the two notes vibrate in the ratio 3 to 2. That is why the tambura drone sounds so settled.
Sa to upper Sa is a full octave, the ratio 2 to 1. Singers say the upper Sa should feel like the same note, only lighter.
Sa Ga Pa outlines the major chord, the brightest-sounding chord there is. Hear Pa before you leap to it.
Coming down by leaps is harder than going up. Aim slightly high in your mind; the voice tends to fall below the target.

stages.title: Your first varasas
stages.about: The first exercises every Carnatic student sings, one line at a time.

chapters.title: Sarali Varasa 1 and 2
chapters.hint: Lines 2 and 4 of every Sarali are the scale you already know, so learn the new lines on their own first.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 1
lessons.swaras: S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali Varasa means 'simple sequence'. Purandara Dasa set these exercises some 500 years ago, and almost every Carnatic singer since began with this one.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 2 - line 1
lessons.swaras: S R S R S R G M
lessons.theory: This line repeats Sa Ri three times before climbing. Sarali Varasas are sung in Adi taalam, the most common rhythm cycle: eight beats to a line.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 2 - line 3
lessons.swaras: S' N S' N S' N D P
lessons.theory: The same pattern from upper Sa downward. Notice it is line 1 turned upside down; most Varasas are built from mirrors like this.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 2
lessons.swaras: S R S R S R G M | S R G M P D N S' | S' N S' N S' N D P | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Your first full Sarali with a pattern in it. Clap on beats 1, 5 and 7 as you sing; that is how Adi taalam is kept: a laghu of four beats and two drutams of two.

chapters.title: Sarali Varasa 3 and 4
chapters.hint: Each new line repeats a short group of notes. Count the groups as you sing.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 3 - line 1
lessons.swaras: S R G S R G S R
lessons.theory: Sa Ri Ga, three times, then Sa Ri. Grouping in threes inside an eight-beat cycle creates a gentle tension that resolves at the line's end.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 3 - line 3
lessons.swaras: S' N D S' N D S' N
lessons.theory: The mirror of line 1. Count the groups in your head: 3, 3, 2.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 3
lessons.swaras: S R G S R G S R | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D S' N D S' N | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali Varasa 3 trains the voice to restart the same group cleanly each time, a skill every gamakam later relies on.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 4 - line 1
lessons.swaras: S R G M S R G M
lessons.theory: Groups of four fit Adi taalam exactly: two groups per line. This makes Sarali 4 feel steady and square.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 4 - line 3
lessons.swaras: S' N D P S' N D P
lessons.theory: Coming down in fours. Keep each upper Sa at the same height every time it returns.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 4
lessons.swaras: S R G M S R G M | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P S' N D P | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Most Carnatic kritis are in Telugu: Tyagaraja, the best-loved composer of all, wrote nearly every one of his in Telugu. These Varasas are the first step toward singing them.

stages.title: Holding and turning
stages.about: A comma holds the note for one more beat. Phrases now turn back before they finish.

chapters.title: Sarali Varasa 5 to 9
chapters.hint: Keep the note steady through every comma.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 5 - line 1
lessons.swaras: S R G M P , S R
lessons.theory: The comma (,) marks a held beat: Pa here lasts two beats. In Telugu notation books the same comma is used, so this is exactly how printed Varasas look.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 5 - line 3
lessons.swaras: S' N D P M , S' N
lessons.theory: Ma is held for two beats on the way down. Holding steady on a note is the foundation of good sruti, staying in tune.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 5
lessons.swaras: S R G M P , S R | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M , S' N | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: The full Sarali 5. The pause on Pa and Ma gives a feeling of breath inside the line; real compositions use held notes the same way.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 6
lessons.swaras: S R G M P D S R | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M G S' N | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 6 climbs to Da, then turns back to Sa Ri. A turn like this is called a prayogam, a characteristic phrase.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 7
lessons.swaras: S R G M P D N D | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M G R G | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 7 climbs to Ni and turns back to Da. The turn just below upper Sa is a favourite move in many ragams.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 8
lessons.swaras: S R G M P M G R | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M P D N | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 8 rises to Pa and walks straight back down. Up-and-back shapes like this train the ear for symmetry.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 9
lessons.swaras: S R G M P M D P | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M P G M | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 9 rises to Pa, dips to Ma, then lifts to Da. Zig-zag movement like this is the first taste of a ragam's twists.

stages.title: Long notes
stages.about: Longer holds and phrases that start from the upper Sa.

chapters.title: Sarali Varasa 10 to 14
chapters.hint: A long note is many beats of the same pitch. Keep it still to the end.

lessons.title: Hold Pa
lessons.theory: Pa held for four beats, twice. Long notes reveal every wobble, so this is where a steady sruti really shows.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 10
lessons.swaras: S R G M P , G M | P , , , P , , , | G M P D N D P M | G M P G M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 10 introduces a full-beat hold on Pa across the whole line. Steady long notes are the resting places of a song, where the listener feels the ragam settle.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 11
lessons.swaras: S' , N D N , D P | D , P M P , P , | G M P D N D P M | G M P G M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 11 begins on upper Sa, the first Varasa that starts high. Start light, as if the note floats.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 12
lessons.swaras: S' S' N D N N D P | D D P M P , P , | G M P D N D P M | G M P G M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 12 doubles some swarams before the held Pa. Repeated notes must each be sung clearly, not merged into one.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 13
lessons.swaras: S R G R G , G M | P M P , D P D , | M P D P D N D P | M P D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 13 mixes holds and turns: Ga is held, then Pa, then Da. It feels close to a real melody; you are almost singing a song.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 14
lessons.swaras: S R G M P , P , | D D P , M M P , | D N S' , S' N D P | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 14 is the last Sarali Varasa. Its held upper Sa in line 3 is the highest long note so far. Completing all fourteen is a real milestone.

stages.title: Twin notes
stages.about: Janta Varasa: every swaram twice, the second with its own fresh stress.

chapters.title: Janta Varasa
chapters.hint: Restart each twin cleanly instead of sliding into it.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 1 - going up
lessons.swaras: S S R R G G M M | P P D D N N S' S'
lessons.theory: Janta is the Telugu word for a pair. Each swaram is sung twice, the second with a fresh push of breath, which builds control for gamakams later.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 1
lessons.swaras: S S R R G G M M | P P D D N N S' S' | S' S' N N D D P P | M M G G R R S S
lessons.theory: The full Janta Varasa 1. Sing the second note of each pair clearly; don't let the pair blur into one long note.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 2 - going up
lessons.swaras: S S R R G G R R | S S R R G G M M | R R G G M M G G | R R G G M M P P | G G M M P P M M | G G M M P P D D | M M P P D D P P | M M P P D D N N | P P D D N N D D | P P D D N N S' S'
lessons.theory: Janta Varasa 2 climbs in overlapping pairs. It is long, so breathe at the end of each eight-beat line.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 2 - coming down
lessons.swaras: S' S' N N D D N N | S' S' N N D D P P | N N D D P P D D | N N D D P P M M | D D P P M M P P | D D P P M M G G | P P M M G G M M | P P M M G G R R | M M G G R R G G | M M G G R R S S
lessons.theory: The descent of Janta Varasa 2. Keep the second note of each pair as strong as the first.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 2
lessons.swaras: S S R R G G R R | S S R R G G M M | R R G G M M G G | R R G G M M P P | G G M M P P M M | G G M M P P D D | M M P P D D P P | M M P P D D N N | P P D D N N D D | P P D D N N S' S' | S' S' N N D D N N | S' S' N N D D P P | N N D D P P D D | N N D D P P M M | D D P P M M P P | D D P P M M G G | P P M M G G M M | P P M M G G R R | M M G G R R G G | M M G G R R S S
lessons.theory: The complete Janta Varasa 2, all twenty lines. Many teachers say Janta Varasas are where a singer's voice first becomes strong.

stages.title: Beyond one octave
stages.about: Step below the lower Sa and above the upper Sa.

chapters.title: Mandra and Tara Sthayi
chapters.hint: Keep the tone the same in every octave. Sing low notes gently and high notes lightly.

lessons.theory: Mandra sthayi is the lower octave, written with a dot below the swaram. Ni below Sa is the first step into it.
A short walk in the lower octave. Let the low notes sound relaxed; low voice comes from ease, not force.
Down to the lower Pa. The middle octave is madhya sthayi; between mandra, madhya and tara, a singer usually covers about two and a half octaves.

lessons.swaras: P. D. N. S R G
lessons.theory: From the lower octave back into the middle one. Moving smoothly across octaves is what makes a voice sound even.
Tara sthayi is the upper octave, written with a dot above. Ri above upper Sa is the first step into it.
A short walk around upper Sa. High notes ring best when the throat stays relaxed and the breath steady.

lessons.swaras: P D N S' R' S' N D P
lessons.theory: Annamacharya of Tallapaka composed thousands of Telugu sankirtanas for Lord Venkateswara in the 15th century. Many of them rise into this upper range at their peak.

stages.title: Rhythm cycles
stages.about: Patterns set to a taalam other than eight beats.

chapters.title: Triputa Taalam Alankaram
chapters.hint: Triputa taalam has seven beats: three, then two, then two.

lessons.title: Triputa Alankaram - going up
lessons.swaras: S R G S R G M | R G M R G M P | G M P G M P D | M P D M P D N | P D N P D N S'
lessons.theory: Alankaram means ornament. Purandara Dasa set seven Alankarams, one for each of the seven suladi taalams, so students learn the rhythms by singing.

lessons.title: Triputa Alankaram - coming down
lessons.swaras: S' N D S' N D P | N D P N D P M | D P M D P M G | P M G P M G R | M G R M G R S
lessons.theory: This Alankaram is in Tisra jaati Triputa taalam: 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 beats. Clap the first beat of each group: 1, 4 and 6.

lessons.title: Triputa Taalam Alankaram
lessons.swaras: S R G S R G M | R G M R G M P | G M P G M P D | M P D M P D N | P D N P D N S' | S' N D S' N D P | N D P N D P M | D P M D P M G | P M G P M G R | M G R M G R S
lessons.theory: The full Triputa Alankaram. The seven suladi taalams combine with five jaatis to make 35 taalams; you have now sung one of them.

stages.title: Picking up speed
stages.about: The same exercises at twice the pace, rendava kaalam. Come here only once the slow versions pass cleanly.

chapters.title: Rendava kaalam (second speed)
chapters.hint: Faster, but every note still lands in tune.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 1 - rendava kaalam
lessons.swaras: S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Carnatic music is sung in three speeds, or kaalams: prathama (first), dwitiya (second) and tritiya (third). Each speed is exactly double the one before.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 3 - rendava kaalam
lessons.swaras: S R G S R G S R | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D S' N D S' N | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 3 at second speed. The groups of three now go by quickly; keep each one clean rather than rushed.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 1 - rendava kaalam
lessons.swaras: S S R R G G M M | P P D D N N S' S' | S' S' N N D D P P | M M G G R R S S
lessons.theory: Janta Varasa at second speed. After this, students usually move on to geethams such as Purandara Dasa's 'Sri Gananatha', their first real songs.
